In the liturgy, Christ’s mystical Body performs public worship: “The whole public worship is performed by the Mystical Body of Jesus Christ, that is, by the Head and His members. Because it… is a sacred action surpassing all others; no other action of the Church can equal its efficacy by the same title and to the same degree.”159

128 In the liturgy the Incarnate Word intercedes for us because He is our Priest, and in us because He is our Head. To Him we pray – He is our God. We must recognize our voice in Him and His in us. We ought to pray with Him, since He prays with us; to pray in Him, since He prays in us.160

129 This participation in the priesthood of Christ is the essence of the sacramental character that begins with Baptism, is perfected with Confirmation and achieves its plenitude in Holy Orders.

130 a) The baptismal character empowers us to receive the other sacraments. It empowers the lay faithful to act as their own proper ministers in the sacrament of matrimony which is the supreme fulfillment of the common priesthood. How we should nurture our soul with the reality of our Baptism! How we should teach this reality to the Christian lay faithful!

131 b) The baptismal character empowers all the baptized to offer the Eucharistic sacrifice. This grandiose and impressive prerogative should be taught insistently to all members of our Institutes who are not ministerial priests. Though they do not carry out the liturgical rite themselves, the baptized participate– in the oblation to the Father of the altar’s Victim in two ways: 1st. They offer the sacrifice by means of the visible priest, since he offers on behalf of all the members when acting in the person of Christ as head and shepherd. 2nd.Together with the visible priest, they unite their acts of praise, supplication, and atonement.

132 c) The character of Confirmation, as it gives us the comforting or corroborative grace, empowers us to profess the faith of Christ with courage and fortitude, and to defend it against its opponents with greater ease and “ex officio,” as it were.

133 d) The character of Holy Orders configures the one ordained with Christ the Head, giving the ministerial priest power over Christ’s physical Body and over His mystical Body. It allows him to act in persona Christi161 – his main act is the immolation and oblation of the sacrifice of the Mass162 – and also to bless, preside, preach, baptize, hear confessions, etc. The members of our Institute who are ministerial priests should return again and again to this ineffable reality which produced an ontological change in them by making them like Christ-the-Head. No “secular spirituality” can reduce their “priestly spirituality.”

Article 3: His Exit From This World a. Passion

134 According to the plan of the most Holy Trinity, it was necessary for Jesus Christ to suffer in order to save all men: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (Jn 3:14-15). Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (Lk 24:26). And he began to teach them that the Son of man must suffer... and be killed, and after three days rise again (Mk 8:31). If in the actual salvific economy Christ’s Passion was necessary, then it will also be necessary for us to suffer. If there were another way to Heaven, Jesus Christ would have followed it, and moreover, He would have taught it. However, He did not. Christ went by means of the royal road of the Holy Cross, and He taught us to go by it as well: If any man would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (Lk 9:23). Saint Cyril of Jerusalem teaches: “Jesus, the Sinless, was crucified for you; and will not you be crucified for Him who was crucified for you?”163

The Cross in Our Life

135 Therefore, we must love the living cross of toils, humiliations, insults, tortures, pains, persecutions, misunderstandings, annoyances, disgraces, scorn, shame, slanders, death... and be able to say with Saint Paul: I die every day (1 Cor 15:31), in order to nail in our hearts the One who was nailed to the cross for us.164

136 We must have an intense desire for the cross: “Grant that we may be ready to die for love of your love, as you died for love of our love.”165 We must pray for this grace: For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should…suffer for his sake (Phil 1:29); and, especially, to ask for the grace of knowledge and joy of the cross which are only achieved in the school of Jesus Christ.

Love of the Cross

137 Therefore, we need a great devotion to the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ: “Everything is in the Passion. There one learns the knowledge of the saints.”166 Love that is not borne from the cross of Christ is weak, “for any part that we look at, either on the part of the person that suffers, or of the things that one suffers, or for the end one suffers them, the cross is the event which is the highest, the most divine and secret that has happened in the world since God created it, neither will it happen until the end of the world.”167 The Cross “was the pulpit of the Preacher, the altar of the Sacrificing Priest, the arena of the Combatant, the workshop of the Wonder-worker.”168 This devotion is realized: with knowledge and love of the gospel stories of the Passion (Mt 26; 27; Mk 14; 15; Lk 22; 23; Jn 18; 19); in the theology of the Passion and Redemption; in the contemplation of the Holy Places of Jerusalem, the crucifixes, the Way of the Cross, the beautiful texts of the “Imitation of Christ” which speak about it,169 the Eucharistic perpetuation of the Passion and Cross – second act of the one drama of the Redemption, the cross in our life that is so well explained in the “Letter to the Friends of the Cross” by Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort; in the fervor to bring the grace of Redemption to all reality: to man, to the whole man and to all men, to married couples and family, to the culture, to political, economic and social life, to the international life of peoples – especially to the problem of peace; in summary, to all the great contemporary problems analyzed in the second part of the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes.170

138 In the Sacred Scriptures we are taught that many men live as enemies of the cross of Christ (Phil 3:18). This is because they reject the cross: and he who does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me (Mt 10:38); they reduce171 and diminish it: Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him (Mt 27:42); they avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ (Gal 6:12); they do not preach the entire message: But if I, brethren, still preach circumcision… In that case the stumbling block of the cross has been removed! (Gal 5:11).

139 The Incarnate Word teaches us to love the Cross: And he said to all…let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (Lk 9:23). We have examples of this from the saints who always carried the sufferings of Jesus in their own bodies,172 completing in themselves what is lacking in the Passion of Christ.173

140 We should not want to know anything except Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Cor 2:2). This doctrine of the Cross174 must be what we preach: the folly of what we preach... Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles (1 Cor 1:21-23). In this cross we must boast, in imitation of the Apostle: But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal 6:14).

141 This Cross prepares for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Cor 4:17), because the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us (Rom 8:18). That is why the Lord Himself encourages us: Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so men persecuted the prophets who were before you (Mt 5:11-12).

142 There is no school greater than the Cross, in which Jesus Christ teaches His disciples how they should be: the Cross is “for us the supreme Pulpit of the truth of God and of man.”175 That is why “in the school brought forth from the Incarnate Word, we understand that accepting his Cross with love is divine wisdom: the cross of the humility of reason in the face of mystery; the cross of the will in the faithful fulfillment of all moral, natural, and revealed law; the cross of one’s own arduous, and at times less than gratifying, duty; the cross of patience in illness and in everyday difficulties; the cross of the tireless zeal to respond to our own vocation; and the cross of the struggle against the passions and attacks of evil.”176 The cross is the Pulpit because in it “the glory of the Love disposed to all has been revealed.”177 The Cross is the only way of life, the sign of the predestined, the scepter of the kingdom of holiness and “the fountain of all blessings; it is the cause of all graces; through it, those who believe receive strength instead of weakness, glory instead of shame, life instead of death.”178

143 The saints of all time, true words of God,179 show us the necessity of the cross in our lives: “Those who suffer for Christ are justly glorified along with Christ as long as they suffer with Him.”180 “Whoever wishes to lead a perfect life needs only to despise what Christ despised on the Cross and to desire what He desired.”181 “Jesus is loved and served on the Cross and crucified with Him, not by any other way.”182

144 Those same saints burned with desire for the Cross: “If the Head is crowned with thorns, can the members expect to be crowned with roses? If the Head is jeered at and covered with dust on the road to Calvary, can the members expect to be sprinkled with perfumes on a throne?”183 “Those who truly love the cross of Christ our Lord find rest when they encounter these trials, and they die when they flee from them or are without them.”184 “To die, Lord, or to suffer.”185 “I want and choose poverty with Christ poor rather than riches, opprobrium with Christ replete with it rather than honors; and to desire to be looked upon as worthless and a fool for Christ, Who first was held as such, rather than wise or prudent in this world.”186 “[This] is for my benefit… Let fire and the cross; let the crowds of wild beasts; let breaking, ripping, and separation of bones; let cutting off of members; let bruising to pieces of the whole body; and let the very torment of the devil come upon me: only let me attain Jesus Christ.”187 “Permit me to be an imitator of the passion of my God.”188 In a word, “Never the Cross without Jesus, nor Jesus without the Cross.”189

145 The saints remind us of the joy that is the fruit of this cross: “I have not been able to suffer, but to me all suffering is sweet.”190 Our hope should be that all pain would give us comfort. Pain “is the fulcrum on which one becomes a lever in order to serve man, as well as to transmit to many others the immense joy of being a Christian.”191

146 The Cross of Christ demands a generous response from us: “[The Passion and the Cross] are a persevering and inflexible aspiration and a cry: an immense cry from the heart.”192 “Jesus, who had never sinned, was crucified for you; and you, won’t you crucify yourself for Him who was nailed to the cross for the love of you?”193 That is why the cross is also “a crown, not an ignominy”194 – because it implies an imitation of Christ. This is the resounding idea: to sacrifice oneself. This is the way history is directed, yet silently directed and in secret.

Benefits

147 From the many benefits that Christ’s Redemption has brought us by His Passion, we should discover:

148 a) how much God loves us, and therefore, how much we should love him: God shows his love for us in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8); I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Gal 2:20).

149 b) the example of the many virtues needed for the salvation of humanity, such as obedience, humility, perseverance, justice and scorn of worldly things. Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps (1 Pt 2:21).

150 c) not only how He redeemed us from sin, but the magnitude of sanctifying grace and of eternal glory that He won for us.

151 d) the great need to be immune from sin: You were bought with a price! (1 Cor 6:20).

152 e) the great dignity of man: though man was conquered by the devil, the devil was conquered by man. Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor 15:57).

153 Briefly, we find a thousand mysteries in the Passion of the Lord, such that its abundance is inexhaustible.

154 We should also attentively consider that Christ wanted to freely suffer all the scathing pains of His Passion and Death; He did not impede them, although He could have: I lay down my life… no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again (Jn 10:17-18). Manifesting all the bodily vigor He had conserved until the last moment, He cried out with a loud voice, and said, “Father, into your hands I commend spirit”; and when he had said this he breathed his last (Lk 23:46).

155 He freely subjected Himself out of obedience to fulfill His Father’s command: So by one man’s obedience, many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19). Certainly obedience is better than sacrifice (1 Sm 15:22), but sacrifice carried out through obedience is supreme perfection. This should teach us how to freely live the vow of obedience, and to never succumb to the false dialectics raised between freedom and obedience, or freedom and authority, or vice versa.

156 Therefore, taking everything into proper consideration, there are two things that are manifested in the Passion: the severity of God who refused to forgive without appropriate satisfaction: He who did not spare his own Son; and His infinite goodness: He handed him over for us all. An unlimited trust in the Father’s overflowing generosity must spring from this: Will he not also give us all things with him (Rom 8:32)?

Example

157 Jesus’ Passion is His second great humiliation: the kenosis of the Passion. In the Passion His humility shines forth. We must imitate it: …but in humility count others better than yourselves (Phil 2:3). In this regard Saint Thomas Aquinas teaches that two things can be considered about man: what is God’s (what pertains to man’s salvation and perfection), and what is man’s (his defects). Now, humility properly considers the reverence whereby man is subject to God. Therefore, every man, with regard to what is his own, should subject himself to every neighbor with regard to what his neighbor has of God: in this subjection, humility shines brightly.195

Ways

158 Contemplating the different ways in which the Passion of the Lord accomplishes its end, that is, the salvation of all people, leads us to admire the following: His infinite wisdom which has done all things well (Mk 7:37); the exquisiteness of His love, He loved them to the end (Jn 13:1); and the magnanimity and generosity of His work, Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Rom 5:20). This masterpiece is the Savior’s most marvelous and exuberant work. It evokes absolute certainty in the salvation carried out by Him, by way of merit, satisfaction, sacrifice, redemption and effectiveness. These five ways of causality that brought about our redemption, far from dismembering it, make us see it with more strength and unity, like fingers that perfect the hand.

159 Christ merited all graces, present and future, without exception, for all people of all ages. His merit is universal: He is the expiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world (1 Jn 2:2). His merit is superabundant, infinite and strictly just.

160 Christ made satisfaction for the sins of all men, offering to the Father a superabundant, universal reparation in strict justice. He bore the sin of man (Is 53:12); God made the sinless one into sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21); having become a curse for us (Gal 3:13); paying for all: Christ Jesus... who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tm 2:6).

161 Christ saved us by the sacrifice of the Cross, a unique oblation: We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb 10:10); a definitive sacrifice: instituted... by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16); an eternal sacrifice, since He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb 7:24). The Victim is perfect: Consequently he is able for all time to save those who draw near to God through him (Heb 7:25). He was simultaneously a sin offering, a peace offering and a holocaust: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph 5:2). Should we not recall here that religious are those who consecrate themselves totally to the service of God by offering themselves to Christ in holocaust?196

162 Christ redeems us from all slavery, since He came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mt 20:28), as a ransom for all (1 Tm 2:6), who gave himself for us to redeem us from all iniquity (Ti 2:14), freeing us from all slaveries of sin, from the punishment due to sin, from death, from the power of the devil and from the mosaic law.

163 Christ is the efficient cause of the objective redemption carried out at Calvary, and of the application of the fruit of the redemption for us (subjective redemption) by faith and the sacraments. He is the most efficient cause of our salvation because He is God, the Word of God, and because His humanity is an instrument united with divinity. Therefore all of Christ’s actions and sufferings instrumentally cause the salvation of mankind.

Effects

164 The effects of His Passion are unfathomable:

1. it frees us from sin: [He] has freed us from our sins by his blood (Rev 1:5);

2. it frees us from the power of the devil: Now shall the ruler of this world be cast out (Jn 12:31);

3. it frees us from the grief of sin: [He] has borne our grief and carried our sorrows (Is 53:4);

4. it reconciles us with God: We were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom 5:10);

5. it opens the doors of Heaven for us: …we have confidence to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus (Heb 10:19);

6. it exalts Christ: God has highly exalted him (Phil 2:9).

165 We now want to highlight an aspect already hinted at. Saint Paul teaches: …In my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Col 1:24). Certainly we do not add anything substantial to the sacrifice of Christ, but in the operative order we somehow complete it. In His sacrifice, Christ-the-Head offered to the Father His own pains and those of all the members of His mystical body; He took upon Himself not only the sins of all men, but also all their pains, which were the sufferings that His members would suffer for His love; these members would be persecuted because they served Him.197 Christ “suffered as our head, and He continues to suffer in his members, that is to say, in us.”198 Therefore, “Christ will be in agony until the end of the world” since “the total measure of all the sufferings of men will not be filled until the end of the world.”199

Suffering

166 Since God chooses suffering to redeem us, it is precious and invaluable when it is endured with patience, accepted as coming from God, and sanctified by uniting it to the pain of Christ. This is the deepest motive for our ministry to the sick, which constantly validates our Christian authenticity. The sick should always be our favored ones!

167 All our sufferings entered into the heart of Christ on Calvary. Those sufferings were offered by Christ, Priest and Victim, in advance. They need to be completed in our flesh. Christ’s sacrifice, prophetically completed in Him, will in fact be completely fulfilled when the number of the elect is completed. We are co-redeemers!

168 The co-redemptive efficacy of our sufferings depends on their union with the Cross, and in the measure and degree of that union. We live from Christ’s sacrifice: no act of virtue is worthy if it is not offered by our Head on the Cross; no sin is forgiven if Christ on Golgotha had not begged mercy for it; no pain is redeeming unless it is united to Christ’s Passion. If we do not learn how to be victims with the Victim, all our sufferings are useless.

169 We must learn how to complete what is missing in the Passion of Christ200 with affective reparation – by prayer and love; effective reparation – fulfilling one’s own duties, apostolate, etc.; and afflictive reparation – by sanctified suffering, for our own spiritual welfare and for the Mystical Body’s.

170 Thus, our Institutes benefit most from their sick members whom we should consider privileged members and for whose good we should be willing to sell “the chalices”201 if necessary.

b. Death on the Cross and Burial

171 Christ kills death with His death; Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? (cf. 1 Cor 15:54-55). Therefore, His death gives life, is a step to His resurrection and our resurrection – both spiritual and corporal.

172 True Christians consider that if we have died with Him, we shall also live with Him (2 Tm 2:11). In baptism we die, and that death ensures our resurrection, if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his (Rom 6:5); offering daily sufferings with Him: sharing in his sufferings, becoming like him in his death (Phil 3:10); and to be able to exclaim, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil 1:21).

173 We “must lead a dying life,”202 or as the poet chants: The one who does not know how to die while he is living / is vain and fool / to die a little every hour / is the way to live / …from death I receive / new life and if I live /I live of so much dying. This is the secret of all supernatural fruitfulness! Everything is in knowing how to die! This is the great science! Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. He who loves his life loses it, and he who hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life (Jn 12:24-25).

174 The cross offers us another magnificent lesson. As we all sinned and perished together in Adam, since sin came into the world through one man… because all men sinned (Rom 5:12), so now in Christ, the new Adam, by the principle of koinonia, we all find salvation and life: Those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ (Rom 5:17).

175 Jesus Christ in Himself assumes the representation of all men: “He suffered for me, he paid for me, and he died for me.”203 In Him we are recapitulated and “concentrated.” Because of this intimate, mysterious identification of Christ with each one of us, He assumes and makes our sins His own: He became sin.204

176 Not only did Jesus die on our behalf, but we also have died, and are represented and contained in Him. Christ and us, us and Christ, form a unique oneness, a compact whole: You are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28). By this mystical identification of persons, we also die on the Cross. Because of this mysterious solidarity or ineffable communion of men with Christ, we have died in radice in Christ.

177 Christ truly died representing all men, so it was necessary that we all, somehow, die in Him and with Him: One has died for all; therefore all have died (2Cor 5:14). Everyone has died in Him. That everyone-dies-because-One-dies supposes that everyone is in that One, and that the One and everyone are the same: We all are one... We should accomplish in deed what was accomplished in radice on the Cross: we must die to our former selves, to sin, to sinful affections and even more, to the very appearance of evil.

178 We must die totally to ourselves. There are three stages for perfect self-denial: external mortification, spirit of sacrifice and total death to oneself. Reaching this third stage is very difficult. We achieve it by means of persistent work. It is to die to live: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:3). The life of Christ was a continuous death whose last act and consummation was the Cross. Christ’s mystical life establishes itself in us by diverse degrees of death:

- death to sins, even to the slightest and the smallest imperfections;

- death to the world and all external things;

- death to the senses and the immoderate care of one’s own body;

- death to one’s character and natural defects: by not speaking or working according to one’s own mood or caprice, by always remaining in peace and in possession of oneself; - death to one’s own will and spirit: subjecting the will to reason, not being led by one’s own desires or fantasies; not becoming obstinate in one’s own judgment; knowing how to listen; being always cheerful with what God gives us;

- death to esteem and love of ourselves: to self-love;

- death to spiritual consolations: one day God will withdraw them completely, and then everything will bother the soul, sicken it and tire it, until one’s nature screams, complains, and becomes furious;

- death to everything that gives support to our soul and to any assurance about the state of our soul: to experience the abandonment of God;

- death to any property concerning holiness: total nakedness. Neither gifts nor virtues are seen, only sins, one’s own nothingness.

179 We should learn how to discover ourselves and others in the Heart and the wounds of Christ. Then we will understand what we pray for when we say, “Within your wounds, hide us,”205 since “we are made Christ.”206

Folly of the Cross

180 In addition, we should keep in mind another reality: the folly of the Cross, for the foolishness of God is wiser than men (1Cor 1:23.25). This folly consists of living “more” and “above”, where all balance, all calculation, all tit-for-tat ceases. This folly begins when there is no longer counting, calculating, weighing, or measuring. Do you only love the one who loves you? Do you only give to the one who can return it to you? Do you only do favors to those who thank you? How great is all that? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? (Mt 5:47).

181 The folly of the Cross consists of living the beatitudes. Blessed be the fools for Christ! They will be pushed around, laughed at and regarded as awkward, slow and even mentally weak. Theirs is the Kingdom of God. Blessed be the fools for Christ! They have stripped themselves and stand before God in their nakedness. Blessed be these fools for Christ! No worldly wisdom will ever be able to deceive them. It is the folly of limitless and immeasurable love. It is to bless those that curse us,207 to repay no one evil for evil (Rom 12:17). When the world says to us, “Look at the fools! They are stoned, and they kiss the hands of those who stone them. They are laughed at and made fun of, and they laugh like senseless children. They are beaten, persecuted and martyred, but they give thanks to God who found them worthy. When the world says all of this, it is a sign that we are doing well. The folly of love! “But the folly of the Cross makes wiser than the wisdom of all men.”

c. The Descent to Hell

182 Saint Peter teaches that Christ went to preach to the spirits in prison (1 Pt 3:19), and that the gospel was preached even to the dead (1 Pt 4:6).

183 The kenosis of the Incarnation of the Word is extended through His Passion and Death, and reaches its fullness when He descends into hell, in such a way that if we stopped believing this truth of our faith, we would somehow be diminishing the reality of the Incarnation.

184 In this mystery Christ showed the fruit of His Passion to the saints of the Old Testament, the Patriarchs and Prophets, Saint Joseph, Saint John the Baptist, the Holy Innocent Martyrs, the good thief... and communicated its glorious holiness to them.

185 He also consoled the souls in Purgatory, taking those that were sufficiently purified. In our preferential option for the poor, we ought to always keep in mind these blessed souls in Purgatory to atone for them.

Article 4: His Glorious Life a. Resurrection The Fact

186 The resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ is a Mystery and a twofold miracle. It is a theological miracle that surpasses the capacity of all created intelligence: If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain (1 Cor 15:14). At the same time, it is an apologetic miracle since the empty tomb and Jesus’ appearances fulfill the prophecies, and the truth of the divinity of Jesus Christ is certified. He is the first-born from the dead (Col 1:18), and the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20). He is the first to resurrect gloriously to an immortal life. He is the beginning of the new creation – re-creation of the world – infinitely superior to the first creation.

Effects

187 The resurrection of Our Lord gave us two main benefits: our future corporeal resurrection and our present spiritual resurrection. We are taught that as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor 15:21), and that He was put to death for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Rom 4:25). It is then evident that justification is the resurrection of souls, who are spiritually dead by sin, dead to the life of grace. Saint Thomas teaches: “The good of grace in one is greater than the good of nature in the whole universe.”208

188 The importance of grace in the saving economy of the New Covenant and the reason why grace is the “only formal cause”209 of our salvation are seen more clearly in the Lord’s resurrection. Sanctifying grace makes us partakers of the divine nature (2 Pt 1:4). As theologians say, it is a physical and formal – though analogous – participation in the divine nature itself. And we were raised up with him (Eph 2:6), becoming “by grace what He is by nature,”210 children of God,211 brethren of Christ. Jesus Christ is the first-born among many brethren (Rom 8:29), and therefore, we are co-heirs with Him, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Rom 8:17). Along with grace we receive the instilled virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Sending Forth of the Holy Spirit: The New Law

189 On the very day of His Resurrection, Jesus Christ did privately what He would do publicly on the day of Pentecost: He sent the Holy Spirit. He breathed on them and said to them, Receive the Holy Spirit (Jn 20:22). The Holy Spirit is the main component of the New Law, also known as New Covenant or Gospel. He is the “abundant life” (Cf. Jn 10:10) that Christ came to bring to the earth. He is the law of Christ (Gal 6:2), the principle of faith (Rom 3:27), the spiritual law,212 the perfect law (Jas 1:25), the law of liberty (Jas 2:12), the law of the Spirit (Rom 8:2), the Gospel of grace (Acts 20:24), and the law of Christ (Gal 6:2). He is the law infused into the heart that Jeremiah prophesied: I will put my law within them, and I will write it upon their hearts (Jer 31:33). He is “whereon all… [the law’s] efficacy is based… the grace itself of the Holy Spirit, which is given to those who believe in Christ.”213 Only this law justifies and saves man: The gospel is the power of God for the salvation to every one who has faith (Rom 1:16). The new law, the Gospel, saves and justifies only as infused – inwardly communicated – not presented as a written text. For that reason Saint Paul says that the letter kills, the Spirit gives life (2 Cor 3:6). By “letter,” Saint Paul means whatever thing or writing exterior to man, even involving spiritual and heavenly matters, like the Gospel writings. Saint Thomas says, “Wherefore the letter, even of the Gospel, would kill, unless there was the inward presence of the healing grace of faith.”214 If this applies to the Holy Gospels authored principally by the Holy Spirit, how much more is this true for this Directory! Without faith in Christ, without the Holy Spirit, without the love of God, without sanctifying grace, all these writings would kill souls since they would remain merely in external things.

190 Living according to the New Law means to live according to the reality that God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit which has been given (Rom 5:5). It is to live according to faith working through love (Gal 5:6), and love never ends (1 Cor 13:8).

Freedom

191 The Resurrection and the sending of the Holy Spirit call us to freedom,215 because for freedom Christ has set us free (Gal 5:1).

192 Freedom implies “building a communion and a participation... upon three inseparable aspects: - the relation of man with the world, as lord;

- with people, as brother;

- and with God, as son.”216

193 “Today they have extended in a great way the range of the abuses of freedom, and this leads to new forms of slavery, very dangerous ones, because they are disguised under the appearance of freedom. This is the paradox, the profound drama of our time: in the name of freedom, slavery is imposed.”217

194 Saint Peter already warned against these abuses, and exhorted the faithful to be truly free without using your freedom as a pretext for evil (1 Pt 2:16), and Saint Paul admonished us not to use freedom as an excuse to serve the flesh.218

195 Authentic freedom identifies with holiness, with the New Law, with the Christian faith and with charity. It is liberty of the children of God (Rom 8:21). Freedom has truth as its foundation as Our Lord showed when He said, the truth will set you free (Jn 8:32). Freedom is characteristic of those who allow the Holy Spirit to lead them: The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (2 Cor 3:17). This is why Saint Augustine teaches, “Love, and do what you will.”219 Saint John of the Cross places freedom at the summit of the mount of perfection, “There is no road here, for there is no law for the righteous man.”220

196 Christian freedom “is to be able to avoid sin and to do meritorious works, without anything having the power to prevent [it]… from reaching the last end.”221

197 We must be free and must know how to form free men and women: “Free... free... free... free... free... free with your freedom... that you may go everywhere with... the holy Gospel in your mouth and the holy Rosary in your hand, to bark like dogs, to burn like embers and to illuminate the darkness of the world like suns.”222

198 Saint Thomas teaches: “Free is he who is the cause of his own action; a servant is he whose cause of action is his master. Therefore, he who acts by his own decision acts freely; he who acts by another agent, does not. Thus, he who avoids evil not because it is evil, but because it is God’s command, is not free; but he who avoids evil because it is evil, that one is free. The Holy Spirit, who makes the soul perfect interiorly through the good habit, accomplishes this. The result is that the soul abstains from evil because of love, as if it were God’s command. Therefore it is called free, not because it rejects divine law, but because it is inclined by good habits to do what is required by the divine law.”223

The New Man

199 The New Law brings us to the New Man by essence, Jesus Christ Himself, that he might create in himself one new man (Eph 2:15) and the new man by participation, namely, all those who are incorporated into Jesus Christ through grace: and put on the new nature, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness (Eph 4:24). The new man is opposed to the old man which…is corrupt through deceitful lusts (Eph 4:22),224 of whom the Apostle prophesied, People will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own likings (2 Tm 4:3).

200 The new man is the “interior man,” strengthened with might through his Spirit (Eph 3:16).225 The new man is also identified with the spiritual man (1 Cor 2:15). He is the man who sings the “new song,” “This new song does not belong to the old man. Only the new man learns it: the man restored from his fallen condition through God’s grace, and now sharing in the new covenant, that is, the kingdom of heaven. To it all our love now aspires and sings a new song. Let us sing a new song not with our lips but with our lives… Every one of us tries to discover how to sing to God. You must sing to him, but you must sing well. He does not want your voice to come harshly to his ears… When will you be able to offer him a perfect performance that you will in no way displease such a supremely discerning listener? See how he himself provides you with a way of singing. Do not search for words, as if you could find a lyric which would give God pleasure. Sing to him ‘with songs of joy.’ This is singing well to God, just singing with songs of joy [which means by] understand[ing] that words cannot express the things that are sung by the heart… Now, who is more worthy of such a cry of jubilation than God himself, whom all words fail to describe? … You must not remain silent, what else can you do but cry out for joy? Your heart must rejoice beyond words, soaring into an immensity of gladness, unrestrained by syllabic bonds.”226

201 Jesus Christ, the supreme and eternal New Man, wants us to assimilate His doctrine, to imitate His examples, to unite ourselves wholeheartedly with His Person and to frequent His sacraments. The modern immanentist conceptions that propose a “new man” – who is no more than a human wretch – detest Jesus by denying man the supernatural dimension of grace. The only thing authentically new that there is, has been, and will be in the world is Jesus Christ who “brought all [possible] novelty, by bringing Himself…”227

202 The new man, the Christian, sings his own song: “The song springs from happiness, and if we look at it well, it is borne from love: working is characteristic of love. The one who knows how to love the new life, also knows how to sing the new song.”228 “For to sing and to intone psalms is the business of those who love.”229 The Christian pilgrimage must be accompanied with song, with manifestations of joy: “So then, my brothers, let us sing now, not in order to enjoy a life of leisure, but in order to lighten our labors. You should sing as wayfarers do sing, but continue your journey. Do not be lazy, but sing to make your journey more enjoyable. Sing, but keep going. What do I mean by keep going? Keep on making progress. This progress must be in virtue; for there are some, the Apostle warns, whose only progress is in vice (Cf. 2 Tim 3:13). If you make progress, you will be continuing your journey, but be sure that your progress is in virtue, true faith and right living. Sing then – but keep going.”230

Joy

203 From the Resurrection of the Lord arises an essential element of our spirituality, and of all Christian spirituality: joy. For us, joy must be manifested in special ways: in the celebration of the Lord’s Day, Sunday; in having a sense of feasting; and in the recreation that we call eutrapelia.

204 Joy, the Christian’s gigantic secret, is spiritual and supernatural, and arises from meditating on the mystery of the Incarnate Word. The angel Gabriel said to Mary, Rejoice, be glad. She would say, My spirit rejoices (Lk 1:47) after Elizabeth had witnessed that the babe in my womb leaped for joy (Lk 1:44). The angel said to the shepherds, I bring you good news of a great joy which will come to all the people (Lk 2:10). Joy is also borne from witnessing the mystery of the Resurrection of the Lord: So they departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy (Mt 28:8). Likewise, the disciples of Emmaus experienced joy: Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road? (Lk 24:32). They could not believe for sheer joy and wonder (Cf. Lk 24:41), and returned... with great joy (Lk 24:52). The disciples were glad when they saw the Lord (Jn 20:20). Saint Paul insists: Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (Phil 4:4).

205 Therefore, the Christian must always be joyful in everything: The kingdom of God is… joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17); may the God of hope fill you with all joy (Rom 15:13); fill you with all joy (Rom 15:32); rejoice (2 Cor 13:11); rejoice in the Lord (Phil 3:1); rejoice always (1 Thes 5:16).

206 The Christian has to be joyful in the practice of virtues: He who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness (Rom 12:8); rejoice in your hope (Rom 12:12); strengthened with all power, according to his glorious might, for all endurance and patience with joy (Col 1:11).

207 The Christian also has to be joyful in sufferings: With all our affliction, I am overjoyed (2 Cor 7:4); as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Cor 6:10); I rejoice in my sufferings (Col 1:24).

208 The Christian must also rejoice in the community of followers of the Risen One: I rejoice over you (Rom 16:19); that my joy would be the joy of you all (2 Cor 2:3); we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith (2 Cor 1:24); always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy (Phil 1:4); my brethren… my joy and crown (Phil 4:1); you are our glory and joy (1 Thes 2:20).

209 The Christian must rejoice in the proclamation of Christ: Christ is proclaimed; and in that I rejoice (Phil 1:18); I shall remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith (Phil 1:25); complete my joy (Phil 2:2); you received the word in much affliction, with joy inspired by the Holy Spirit (1 Thes 1:6).

210 Ultimately, joy springs from believing that God is;231 that Christ is, Take heart, it is I (Mk 6:50); that truth prevails over lies, good over evil, beauty over ugliness, love over hate, peace over war, mercy over vengeance, life over death, grace over sin... in short, being over nothingness, the Virgin over Satan, Christ over the Antichrist, God over all. “God is infinite joy.”232

Sunday

211 Derived from the Paschal Mystery and from the Lord’s Day, on Sunday – the feast day par excellence – feasts should arise among us, because authentic feasting is born from worship – praise given to the Creator for the goodness of existence. On the seventh day God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good…and he rested (Gn 1:31, 2:2-3). Saint Augustine teaches that worship takes place by means of the “offering of praise and thanksgiving.”233 Since sacrifice is the main act of worship, it is the “soul” of the feast. How much more meaningful this becomes under the light of the Lord’s Resurrection and the perpetuation of His Sacrifice on the altars! Indeed, by the Incarnation of the Word and His Paschal Mystery, man is elevated to a super-eminent plane, the plane of grace that absolutely exceeds the order of nature. Therefore the Paschal Mystery with Sunday, its continuation, is the source of authentic feasting. On Sundays we celebrate the goodness of this “superior existence” brought by the Word, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (Jn 1:17), as well as the hope of being able to finally enter Eternal Life, the true Feast. The Paschal Mystery and Sunday signify and anticipate this true Feast. The name Eucharist, given by Christian tradition to the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, refers to this action of thanksgiving. Sunday already immerses us into the true and eternal feast. For us who live here, our feasts are an opening to that life. We go from feast to feast toward the Feast.234

Feasting

212 All feasts participate from the Lord’s Resurrection and from Sunday, since the motive of the feast is joy: “Feast is joy and nothing else.”235 But joy supposes a foundation, something that makes one joyful; it is the response of a lover who possesses what he loves. One becomes joyful because he possesses the good that is appropriate to him, either in reality, or in hope, or at least in memory. Only the one who is joyful in love is truly joyful: “Where charity is joyful, there is festivity.”236 Therefore, there is no greater motive for joy than the Resurrection of the Lord because His triumph is our triumph, His victory is our victory. The Paschal Mystery is the manifestation par excellence of the love of God for men: He loved them to the end (Jn 13:1). We must be joyful in this mystery, and our joy must be permanent. Therefore our Institutes must appropriately celebrate the great solemnities, especially the Octave of Easter, Sundays, and the feast days of Our Lady and of the Apostles.

213 There is another kind of minor feast: recreation, where the virtue of eutrapelia has to be practiced. The soul, like the body, becomes tired and has to rest. Delectation is rest for the soul, by remedying its fatigue. It gives pause to the tension of the spirit. Therefore, we must grant this rest to the soul by means of games and feasts, whose moderation springs from the virtue of eutrapelia, practiced during the times of recreation.

214 Whoever does not practice the virtue of eutrapelia with gladness will hardly persevere. It is necessary to guard oneself against those, who under the appearance of virtue, do not want to practice the virtue of eutrapelia. They are usually led by their selfishness, they offend their neighbor and are very judgmental. And what is worse, they go against the truth of man, who is intelligent and therefore has to be playful.

Sending Forth and Mission

215 As the four evangelists point out, the Resurrected Christ commands us to mission: As the Father has sent me, even so I send you (Jn 20:21). This mission requires us to testify, You are witnesses of these things (Lk 24:48); to address, by the power of the Lord, all nations of the world: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations (Mt 28:19), all the world (Mk 16:15); to preach the Gospel; to teach others to observe what He ordered us; to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that he who believes will be saved, with Christ accompanying us to the close of the age (Mt 28:20).

216 So as not to dodge the missionary adventure237 and at the same time, to move many others toward it, we need to be like poets, for only poets move people. What bigger poet is there than Jesus Christ?! What greater poetry is there than shouting, “Put out into deep water – Duc in altum!”238 What profound words, with such deep content, a deep mystical resonance that impels one toward great ideals. These words are understood by men of action, with broad vision and with decisive and generous hearts. They are understood by men who, because of their soul’s nobility, smile with joy in knowing that Jesus Himself tells them: Duc in altum! It is an invitation to accomplish great works, extraordinary undertakings involving a great deal of adventure, vertigo, danger, where the waves shake the boat, the salty water sprinkles the face, the prow makes way for the first time, where there is no trail and stars are the only reference, where the keel of a ship is shaken by the whirling waters, where the deployed sails endure the wind’s furor, where the masts crack… and the soul shivers. Into deep water! Far from the shore and the mainland of mere human calculations and cold thoughts… where the water moves, the heart beats quickly, where the soul knows celestial bliss and fascinating joys. To “put out into the deep” is to take the demands of the Gospel seriously and thoroughly: Go, sell what you possess (Mt 19:21). It is the longing of our restless heart, yearning to possess the Infinite. It is the impetus of the saints and martyrs who gave everything for God. It is characteristic of fishermen, humble, hardworking men who do not fear dangers; vigilant and patient during long vigils, consistent in repeating their outings on the sea, prudent to catch fish, hardened by the salt and the sun. It is being willing to die, like the grain of wheat, in order to see Christ in all things. We make ours the ardent words of Blessed Louis Orione: “Whoever does not want to be an apostle leaves the Congregation: today, whoever is not an apostle of Jesus Christ and the Church is an apostate.”239

b. Ascension

217 Christ’s Ascension to Heaven moves us to always look for the essential things, invisible to the eyes of the body, that do not pass away and do not die: Seek the things that are above, where Christ is… Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth (Col 3:1-2).

218 In these times of crude temporalism, when many contemporaries are infected with secularism, we must give the clear testimony of men who are not encased within the horizons of this world, even when we are involved in the unavoidable commitment of the promotion of justice.

219 The Lord’s Ascension must fill us with unshakable hope. He assured us, In my Father’s house are many rooms… I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also (Jn 14:2-3). “The members must follow whither the Head has gone.”240 His Ascension is the cause of ours. “Christ with us is a single thing.”241 All with Christ “form a single Christ.”242 Our commonwealth is in heaven (Phil 3:20).

220 While he was going…they were gazing heavenward (Acts 1:10). Our Institute will always have a preferential place for the contemplative branches. The contemplative life, as Blessed John Paul II teaches, is “the nucleus starting from where you prepare to give a full sense to your religious life, as ambassadors of Christ243 amidst this world.”244 This is because life implies a permanent dedication to God and to believing and loving His mystery and His plan of salvation for all men, as Saint Paul writes: Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God… you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:1-3). Blessed John Paul II says: “To be devoted to God is... the noblest and highest form of activity for the human being, insofar as this concentrates completely on the adoration of the Infinite Being who desires the salvation of all humanity... you have here, thus, the precise form of collaboration that... you offer to the Church for the good of souls.”245 Saint John of the Cross says: “Let those men of zeal, who think that by their preaching and exterior works they convert the world, consider that they would be much more edifying to the Church, and more pleasing unto God, by setting aside the good example they would give and spending at least one half their time in prayer… Certainly they would do more, and with less trouble… To act otherwise is to beat the air, to do little more than nothing, sometimes nothing and occasionally even mischief.”246 In the words of Saint Teresa of the Child Jesus: “Only this Jesus claims of us. He doesn’t need our works, but only our love.”247 Thanks to the prayer and the sacrifice of those who consecrate themselves to God in contemplative life, the Lord raises up preachers, confessors, spiritual directors, etc., who transmit the truth to men. We can truly say that other people transmit what the contemplatives contemplate.

c. To the Right Hand of the Father

221 He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb 1:3), which, according to Saint John Damascene, means “the glory and the honor of the divinity.”248 In other words, Christ reigns together with the Father and has judicial power over the living and the dead. Knowing that the Lord is at the Father’s right hand should make us trust in Him greatly: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil 4:13). Another magnificent expression of total trust is Saint Paul’s I know the one in whom I have put my trust (2 Tm 1:12).

d. The Kingship of Christ

222 The Lord is King over all humanity in a strict, literal and proper sense since He received from the Father dominion and glory and kingship (Dn 7:14). He is King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev 19:16). The foundation of this kingship is four-fold: first, it belongs appropriately to Him as God, the Incarnate Word. Saint Cyril of Alexandria says: “Christ obtains the dominance over all creatures, not taken by force nor taken by any other reason, but by his very essence and nature.”249 Second, it belongs to Him by virtue of Redemption, by right of conquest, since He bought us with His blood: You know that you were ransomed…... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pt 1:18-19). Third, it belongs to Him because He is the Head of the Church and by the fullness of grace: full of grace and truth (Jn 1:14). Fourth, it belongs to Him by right of inheritance: whom he appointed the heir of all things (Heb 1:2). His royal authority includes the fullness of the threefold power: legislative, judicial and executive.

223 The scope of His reign is twofold: personal and social. He reigns over all intelligence because He is the Truth, “and it is from him that truth must be obediently received by all mankind.”250 He reigns over all will because He is Goodness, “and further by his grace and inspiration he so subjects our free will as to incite us to the most noble endeavors.”251 In addition, He reigns over all hearts because He is Love. His reign is also a social one. “There is no difference in this matter between the individual and the family or the State; for all men, whether collectively or individually, are under the dominion of Christ. In him is the salvation of the individual, in him is the salvation of society.”252

224 His Kingdom is neither temporary nor earthly, My kingship is not of this world (Jn 18:36), but eternal, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Lk 1:33), and universal, all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Mt 28:18); His is a kingdom of truth and life, of sanctity and grace, of justice, love and peace.253

225 All missionary and apostolic work is based on the conviction that Christ must reign (1Cor 15:25).

Article 5: His Mystical Life a. The Church, the Mystical Body

226 Beginning with His Resurrection, and forever thereafter, the sacred humanity of Jesus Christ lives a glorious and immortal life; from the moment of the Ascension, His humanity is in Heaven and will return with His Second Coming.

227 Meanwhile, in the intervening centuries between His Ascension and His Second Coming, Jesus lives His mystical life on earth. The Word assumed a human nature to accomplish the design of salvation. He now chooses other human natures in order to extend that design through time, so that salvation may reach all men of all times. The Church is Jesus Christ continued, diffused and communicated. The Church is the extension of the redemptive Incarnation, by means of the three-fold function: prophetic, priestly and royal. She is the new People of God. She is “in Christ, the nature of sacrament – a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and of unity among all men”254; she is an organically structured community;255 “a people united in the unity of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”256 The Church is mystery, communion and mission.257 Belonging to Her – by faith and baptism – must be our seal of honor. By the light of the Word of God, the Church always celebrates the mysteries of Christ for the salvation of the world.258

b. Her “History”

228 The reality of the Church-mystery precedes the creation of the world, as Saint Clement of Rome says: “The Church is not now, but from before,”259 and the Shepherd of Hermes: “She was created... before all things... by reason of her the world was ordered.”260

229 In a mediate manner, “This Church was prepared in marvelous fashion in the history of the people of Israel and in the ancient Covenant”;261 in an immediate way “established in this last age of the world”262 by Jesus Christ. He gave her the doctrine, the sacraments, and the hierarchy; in a special way in Peter, by whom He begins her constitution when professing: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Mt 16:18). Jesus culminates her preparation on Calvary, when blood and water flowed from the wounded side of Christ crucified; “as often as the sacrifice of the cross by which Christ our Passover is sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7) is celebrated on the altar, the work of our redemption is carried out.”263 The Church was openly “made manifest in the outpouring of the Spirit”264 in the Jewish Pentecost265 and in the pagan Pentecost.266 She “will be perfected gloriously at the end of times,267 when all the just, “from Abel the Just until the last elect,”268 are united before the Father in one Universal Church.

230 We must always keep this in mind so that we do not succumb to the temptation of thinking that the Church begins with us. Not only are there 2,000 years of history on our shoulders, but also the world’s entire past and future.

c. Her “Soul”: the Holy Spirit

231 The Holy Spirit plays a constitutive, fundamental, essential role in the Church. Indeed, the Holy Spirit accomplishes our incorporation into the mystical Body of Christ, which we belong to through baptism. We must be reborn of water and Spirit;269 by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Cor 12:13).

232 The Holy Spirit was already revealed in the Old Testament, though not as a Divine Person. He was revealed under different aspects which related both to the life of Israel, and to the life of its individual members. The Holy Spirit acts in creation.270 He is the source of life: I will pour my Spirit upon your descendants…they shall spring up like grass amid waters (Is 44:3- 4). He is the guiding principle of both Israel as well as the prophecy of the future Messiah: Then the Lord came down in the cloud and spoke to him, and took some of the spirit that was upon him and put it upon the seventy elders (Nm 11:25); And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord. And his delight shall be in the fear of the Lord (Is 11:2-3); I have put my Spirit upon him (Is 42:1). By His action the prophets spoke: And when the spirit rested upon them, they prophesied (Nm 11:25). His action renews, purifies the heart, and sanctifies: Take not thy holy Spirit from me ... put a new and right spirit within me… purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Ps 51:9.12.13).

233 In the New Testament all these aspects are taken up and acquire new meaning in the light of Jesus’ revelation of the Holy Spirit as a Divine Person, who is present in the very life of the Incarnate Word in a most special way. The Spirit is author of the hypostatic union which is called “grace of union”;271 therefore, the Incarnation is His work: The Holy Spirit will come upon you (Lk 1:35). Henceforth, Christ “is the supreme wonder carried out by the Holy Spirit.”272 As we profess in the Creed, “He was conceived by the Holy Spirit”273 – “by the power of the Spirit.”274 This same Spirit is the author of Jesus’ holiness: Therefore the child to be born will be called holy (Lk 1:35). The response of the Blessed Virgin, from which the Incarnation followed, is a fruit of the Holy Spirit’s action in her soul.275 His action establishes a most personal relationship, a spousal and nuptial union with Her. That union is a model for us,276 since the Spirit dwells in us (Cf. 1 Cor 3:16), and in every soul in grace. The Spirit is also present in Jesus’ prayer and messianic preaching. Christ applies the fulfillment of the prophecy of Is 61:1 to Himself: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord (Lk 4:18.19). The Spirit is the source of Christ’s joy: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit (Lk 10:21). From the Holy Spirit Christ has the power to expel demons: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Mt 12:28). The Spirit is present in His redeeming Sacrifice, which Jesus calls “baptism”: Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized? (Mk 10:38); I came to cast fire upon the earth; and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how I am constrained until it is accomplished! (Lk 12:49.50). John the Baptist had already announced that he who is coming after me…will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire (Mt 3:11); and we are taught that through the eternal Spirit [He] offered himself without blemish to God (Heb 9:14). Finally, the Holy Spirit is author of the Resurrection of Christ: Being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit (1 Pt 3:18). Here, the Holy Spirit manifests Himself as Life-Giver, “Lord and giver of life,”277 as we profess in the Nicene Creed. The Gospel, the New Law, consists of the Holy Spirit’s grace; that is why it is “the law of life”: The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death (Rom 8:2).

234 After Jesus’ Resurrection and Ascension into Heaven, the Spirit is sent to the Church, according to the promise of the Lord: When the Counselor comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness to me (Jn 15:26). “Once the Lord Jesus was exalted on the cross and glorified, the Spirit that had been promised was poured out, by the one which called and congregated in unity of faith, hope, and charity to the people of the New Testament which is the Church.”278 This sending forth was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost: All were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:1-4). Therefore, the Holy Spirit is a gift given by God to the Church: You will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38). The Holy Spirit is a gift that vivifies the Church: Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (Jn 4:10). The Holy Spirit vivifies the Church so much so that it is correctly called the “Soul of the Church.” The Spirit “gives life to, unifies and moves the whole body. The Church Fathers compared His work to the function that the soul, principle of life, fulfills in the human body.”279 Therefore, the Holy Spirit is the source of the Church’s unity: By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Cor 12:13); this unity is based on charity, also a fruit of the Spirit’s action: God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit which has been given to us (Rom 5:5). Saint Augustine rightly called the Holy Spirit, “Kiss, Love, Knot of union between the Father and the Son.”280 The Spirit is also the source of the Church’s holiness, since He is Holy: Spirit of holiness (Rom 1:4), performing the work of sanctification: God chose you…through sanctification by the Spirit (2 Thes 2:13).

235 The Holy Spirit performs this sanctification inwardly in our hearts: God’s Spirit dwells in you (1 Cor 3:16). By this renewing presence the Holy Spirit transforms us, making us children of God: Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So through God you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir (Gal 4:6-7). All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Rom 8:14ff). The Holy Spirit renews us, makes us new creatures made by God: You also are built into it for a dwelling place of God in the Spirit (Eph 2:22). By this renewal and purification, we can have access to the Father in the Holy Spirit: For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Eph 2:18). He is the guarantee of eternal life: Sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, which is the guarantee of our inheritance (Eph 1:13-14). He teaches us all things, because the Holy Spirit examines all,281 He will teach you all the things (Jn 14:26). He is the Spirit of Truth (Jn 14:17). He is our helper: The Spirit helps us in our weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with sighs too deep for words (Rom 8:26). He enriches the Church with the diversity of His gifts: All these are inspired by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Cor 12:11). Therefore, we must always ask the Lord to grant us His Holy Spirit, and docility to Him, so that we may belong to Christ more and more, and therefore to His mystical Body, since any one who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Rom 8:9). God never denies this most valuable gift which the whole New Law consists of, and therefore, our salvation consists of: If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! (Lk 11:13). We must then understand that the kingdom of God is… righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17).

The Word of God

236 The Holy Spirit is the Principal Author of Sacred Scripture because He wants us to have our fill at “the table of the Word.”282 “The Holy Spirit begot Sacred Scripture with more abundant truth than men can understand.”283 The Bible is closely united to the mystery of the Incarnate Word, “For as the substantial Word of God became like to men in all things, ‘except sin,’ so the words of God, expressed in human language, are made like to human speech in every respect, except error.”284

237 The wealth of this heavenly treasure285 of the Word of God is seen, among other things, by the fact that it is:

contained in the Holy Books,

celebrated in the Holy Liturgy,

commented by the Church Fathers,

witnessed by the martyrs,

deepened by the Doctors,

genuinely interpreted by the Church Magisterium,

and lived by the saints of all times.

238 The Word of God must be “deepened in the Church,”286 with the same Spirit in which it was written.287 This is precisely our Institute’s true strength, “as it is its supreme sacramental proclamation in the Eucharistic Sacrifice.”288

239 Sacred Scripture must be the “soul of our soul,” of our spirituality, theology, preaching, catechesis and pastoral work. What Saint Jerome said about an acquaintance should also be said of us, “Indeed by constant reading and long-continued meditation, he had made his breast a library of Christ,”289 since for us, “The Word of God is nothing less than the Body of Christ.”290

d. One Church

240 “This is the only one Church of Christ, which in the Creed we profess to be one, holy, catholic and apostolic.”291

241 The Church of Christ is one and only. The idea of koinonia (communion) adequately expresses the profound nucleus of the Church’s Mystery, because it is the mystery of the personal union of each man with the Holy Trinity and with other men, beginning with faith and baptism.

242 This common union includes both a vertical dimension – communion with God – and a horizontal dimension – communion with men. This unity is a gift from God, a fruit of the divine initiative accomplished in the Paschal Mystery.

243 Ecclesial communion is both invisible and visible. As the invisible reality, it is the communion of each man: with the Father through Christ in the Holy Spirit; with other men, who also participate in sanctifying grace;292 in the Passion of Christ;293 in the same faith;294 in the same Spirit.295 This invisible reality maintains an intimate relationship with the visible communion founded upon the doctrine of the Apostles, the sacraments and the hierarchical order. This relationship between the visible and invisible aspects of ecclesial communion is a constitutive element of the Church “as the universal Sacrament of salvation.”296

244 This hierarchical and mystical reality – visible and spiritual, terrestrial and celestial, canonical and charismatic, human and divine – resembles “the mystery of the Incarnate Word”297 by way of a deep analogy since “the same Christ is embodied in his Body, the Church.”298 Therefore, we who are proud to call ourselves religious of the Incarnate Word would gravely betray our charism if we did not work to have an authentic ecclesial spirituality that incorporates us fully into the Church of the Incarnate Word. We do not want to know anything apart from her.

245 The most solid unity goes hand-in-hand with a diversity that does not block unity and makes it a communion. The Church’s universality in “the unity of faith and [its] only divine structure,”299 accepts the plurality of ministries, charisms, ways of life and apostolate, diverse liturgical and cultural traditions, theologies, spiritualities and disciplines. This reality admirably shows “the catholicity of the undivided Church.”300

246 We must be fervent promoters “of the unity that does not block diversity, as well as... a diversity that does not block unity, but enriches it.”301 We are called daily to edify, respect and safeguard this unity-in-diversity, especially by means of that love which is the bond of perfection (Col 3:14). As the Angelic doctor said, “The Church is one... by the unity of charity, since all are united in loving God, and bound to one another in mutual love.”302

247 Religious institutes are an expression of this unity-indiversity, and we wish to be numbered among them. Although they do not belong to the Church’s hierarchical structure, they belong “undeniably to her life and holiness.”303 When institutes have a supra-diocesan character, rooted in the Petrine ministry, they also work together for communion among the various local Churches. Our experience has allowed us to see the importance of this truth for our spirituality.

Agree With One Another

248 We aspire, according to the words of Saint Paul, to agree with one another (2 Cor 13:11) in the Lord (Phil 4:2). This unanimity or concordance we seek means unity in the judgment of reason about what must be done and unity in the will so that all may want the same thing. This concordance is born of the same faith by which we know what must be done, and from charity by which we all love the same goods and share the same burdens like good soldiers of Jesus Christ.304 This union exists because we all feel the same about God, since wisdom – the sweet-tasting knowledge of divine things – reigns among all. It is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age… But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God (1 Cor 2:6-7). Only the crucified Jesus Christ can grant this wisdom, to those who are called… the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24).

249 The Kingdom of God becomes present in this harmony with one another (Rom 12:16), since “the kingdom’s nature, therefore, is one of communion among all human beings with one another and with God.”305

250 This supposes that each member of our Religious Family not only rejoices in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17) with the good he possesses, but also that each tends unceasingly toward a greater perfection: Brethren, I do not consider that I have made it my own; but one thing I do, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Phil 3:13).

251 This also presumes that everyone casts aside everything that impedes or distorts this unanimity of agreement. The first thing we must cast aside is pride, a pride that drives us to inordinately seek our own excellence, and to refuse to submit to others or to recognize their excellence. Pride produces discord: By insolence the heedless make strife (Prv 13:10). Another obstacle to this unanimity of agreement is the presumption of wisdom, thinking oneself to be self-sufficient, thereby refusing other’s teachings, which is contrary to St. Paul’s example: I went up by revelation; and I laid before them (but privately before those who were of repute) the gospel I preach among the Gentiles, lest somehow I should be running or had run in vain (Gal 2:2).

252 The Holy Spirit poured into our hearts – the New Law – makes us maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph 4:3). Through love, He removes us from selfishness, individualism, a spirit of opposition and distrust, a spirit of unwillingness, of non-participation, of non-consent with others. The Spirit of Christ is the Spirit of communion: Live in harmony with one another (Rom 12:16), in such a way that we will truly care for others: that the members may have the same care for one another (1 Cor 12:25). Hence, in our communities, which must demonstrate a unity among people and a body full of thinking members – no one should behave as if he is all on his own, as a self-sufficient “nomad.” We should learn to act like the parts or members of a whole.

253 Submissiveness and servility are also destructive of this union. These traits sacrifice truth and one’s own conscience by seeking a false peace, or by not admonishing a friend, or by avoiding some problem or, on occasion, by taking advantage of a situation by silence or applause. Whoever does such things resembles those Jews that believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees, they did not confess it, lest they should be put out of the synagogue: for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God (Jn 12: 42-43).

254 The fruit of this “agreement-in-the-Lord” is peace: The harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace (Jas 3:18). True peace, given by Christ,306 is tranquility in order. It arises naturally when everyone, by faith and charity, is ordained to God. Along with peace, another fruit of this harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus (Rom 15:5) is the unity that reigns among all, even in the least details of daily life or any decision. This is possible because each person has the certainty that in everything we do, we will seek the glory of God, with a single heart and a single soul.307

e. The Holy Church

255 The Church is the Communion of Saints.308 It is a common union attained by visibly participating in the holy goods, especially the Eucharist, the root of the common, invisible union of the participants, the saints. There is a spiritual koinonia among members of the same Body that leads to an effective union in charity and prayer. This koinonia exists not only among the pilgrims still on Earth, but also between them and those who have arrived in Heaven or are in Purgatory, on their way to Heaven.

256 There is a mutual relationship between the diverse stages of the one Church. This mutual relationship is founded on: the intercession of Christ for us: He always lives to intercede for us (Heb 7:25); the intercession of the saints to whom “we are most closely united”;309 the example of the saints who “spur us to seek the future city… the perfect union with Christ, holiness”;310 the intercession of the Holy Virgin Mary in “whose protection the faithful take refuge together in prayer in all their perils and needs.”311 This is why a profound devotion to the saints responds to the reality of the Church as mystery-of-communion.

257 The saints are eloquent signs of the Church’s vitality. By embodying the Church’s mark of holiness, they are an apologetic asset of the truth of our faith. They are the best members of the mystical Body of Christ, the best and most complete fruit of the Incarnation and the Redemption. Therefore, they transform the world with their example and with the power of their intercession. They constantly remind us of Heaven, eternal life, and the reward of merits: God Himself! In honoring them, we honor God, because the saints are His masterpieces, and by “crowning their merits, the Lord crowns His own gifts.”312 Even after their death, they fulfill posthumous missions, pushing whole generations to the heroism of following Jesus Christ, being not only to the young but to the great body of his nation.... example of nobility and a memorial of courage (2 Mac 6:31). That is why there is no historical record more complete, more magnificent, and more beneficial than the Litany of the Saints, which evokes and invokes all the great souls who have illuminated our earth and who have advanced humanity with their virtues. We must venerate their relics, which never stop working.

258 Therefore, for our part, we must do everything possible to assure that the face of the Church be without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish (Eph 5:27). We must always remember the irreplaceable importance of sanctifying grace, given by the worthy reception of sacraments, the “divine relics of the Incarnation.”313

f. Catholic Church

259 The Church of Christ is the universal community of the Lord’s disciples that extends to all times, places, races, languages and cultures. This is what “Catholic” means.

260 The Church is “Catholic” also in her doctrine. Some people emphasize the teachings of Saint John, others emphasize those of Saint Paul, etc. There is a variety of theological schools. There are different venerable liturgical rites, and we wish our Institute to have an “Oriental Branch” to help our brothers of the Eastern Churches, since they are part of the “undivided heritage of the universal Church.”314 We must not succumb to localism, reductionism, partialities, or unilateralism that threaten catholicity. The Catholic Church breathes with two lungs: “One cannot breathe like a Christian, or better said as a Catholic, with a single lung; it is necessary to have two lungs, that is to say, the Eastern and the Western.”315

261 The universal Church is “a corporate body of Churches”;316 therefore, it is a communion of local Churches. They are “parts... of the only Church of Christ”;317 they are constituted “after the model of the universal Church”;318 in them “is found and operates the true Church of Christ, which is One, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic.”319 They have a special relationship of “mutual interiority”320 with the universal Church. The universal Church, in its essential mystery, is both an ontological and chronological reality, prior to each specific and concrete Church. The Church-mystery is mother of the specific Churches, her daughters.

262 We do not belong to the universal Church through the mediation of a particular Church. By faith and baptism we are directly incorporated into the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, although entrance and life in the universal Church are necessarily carried out in a specific Church. Therefore, no one is a stranger in the Church.321 He who belongs to a particular Church belongs to all the Churches – without disrupting canonical dependence.322 Belonging to the Communion of the Church is never exclusively specific, but rather – due to its nature – is in itself always universal: “He who is in Rome deems the Indians as her members.”323

Missionary and Ecumenical Church
