263 Since the universal Church is “the universal Sacrament of salvation,”324 she is open – not closed – to missionary and ecumenical dynamics; she has been sent to announce and to testify, to enact and to extend the mystery of the communion that is constitutive of her; to gather all and everything in Christ.325 As an image of the Church, our small Religious Family must never be closed off, but rather must be open like the arms of Christ on the Cross that were “dislocated” for love’s sake.

264 The Holy Spirit, present and acting in every time and place, acts “in the heart of every person, through the ‘seeds of the Word,’ to be found in human initiatives – including religious ones – and in mankind’s efforts to attain truth, goodness, and God Himself.”326 Our mission, therefore, is to joyfully and respectfully discover these seeds, so that men may awaken to a stronger desire of truth and charity,327 since “the Holy Spirit in a manner known only to God offers to every man the possibility of being associated with this paschal mystery.”328

265 This presence of the Spirit “affects not only individuals, but also society and history, peoples, cultures, and religions… [it] is the Spirit who sows the ‘seeds of the Word’ present in various customs and cultures, preparing them for full maturity in Christ,”329 because the Holy Spirit already worked in the world before Christ was glorified.330

266 This work of the Holy Spirit is an evangelical preparation and “can only be understood in relation to Christ, the Word who took flesh by the power of the Spirit.”331 Consequently, it “is not to be separated from His particular activity within the body of Christ, the Church.”332

267 Therefore, the teaching of Saint Ambrose, “all that is true, said by any person, comes from the Holy Spirit,”333 will forever be like a torch that illuminates our work. The saints affirmed and believed that, “Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians”;334 “that all good Christians understand that whatever truth, wherever truth may be found, belongs to his Master”;335 “no one can say anything true [of his own accord], but only moved by the Holy Spirit who is Spirit of Truth”;336 “there is no knowledge of the truth but only in the Holy Spirit who works in the intelligence and preserves it”;337 “all which is good and all which is true is from the Holy Spirit.”338

268 Thanks to the teaching of Christ, we know that there is a humanity that opposes faith and the gift of grace, called the “world”339 by the Lord Himself. Facing this “world” – to which Christ sends us as sheep in the midst of wolves (Mt 10:16) – Saint Paul admonishes: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2). However, this difference from the “world” does not mean that we are afraid of the “world,” or contemptuous of it,340 since if one is conscious of what the Lord wants, the duty of evangelization and the urgency of the mission become apparent. Therefore, a merely conservative attitude is not enough, but rather the diffusion and the announcement of the deposit of the faith are necessary, according to the command of Christ. Dialogue is the name we give to “this internal drive of charity which seeks expression in the external gift of charity.”341

269 This dialogue, which is a spiritual communication, has its transcendent origin in God Himself: “In the Incarnation and in the Gospel, it is God’s Word that speaks to us.”342 Such a dialogue of God with men is born from divine love and is directed to all men without forcing anyone.

270 We must know and “adopt the way of life of ordinary people in all that is human and honorable”,343 without succumbing to the danger of weakening or diminishing the truth, since “an immoderate desire to make peace and sink differences at all costs (irenism and syncretism) is ultimately nothing more than skepticism about the power and content of the Word of God which we desire to preach.”344 “The effective apostle is the man who is completely faithful to Christ’s teaching. He alone can remain unaffected by the errors of the world around him, the man who lives his Christian life to the full.”345

271 Preaching has particular importance. It must always be “skillfully expressed, carefully thought-out, and zealously imparted. May it be supported by the evidence of real virtue. Progress must be its aim. It must concern itself with imparting a sure faith.”346

272 Although this dialogue embraces all men, four environments, or “circles,” are distinguished in which this spiritual communication is carried out, according to the different attitudes of people:

273 The first circle is of those with whom we share human values, in order to elevate them to the supernatural and Christian level.347 Most striking in this environment is the problem of atheism, founded on false theories and not consisting of “a liberating force, but a catastrophic one, for it seeks to quench the light of the living God.”348 Dialogue is especially difficult in these circumstances, and “we must come to a prudent decision about them, and answer them effectively,”349 and we must know that there are many situations that are occasions for such dialogue.

274 The second circle is of those who worship one God. Among them are Jews, Muslims and the faithful from African and Asian religions. Aware that the true religion is Christianity, and yearning for all those who seek God to recognize it as such, we must recognize the many spiritual and moral values that they possess, and the ideals that can be promoted and defended in common.350

275 The third circle “comprises all those who take their name from Christ. In our dialogues, we should first stress what unites us, and then what divides us.” We must demonstrate how those elements of the Church that may look like obstacles for union are fruits of the will of Christ for the benefit, unity and freedom of all. In particular, we need to demonstrate that the Primacy of Peter perpetuated in the Pope is not an obstacle: “Take away the sovereign Pontiff, and the Catholic Church would no longer be Catholic.”351 Without the Roman Pontiff “we shall have as many schisms in the Churches as there are priests.”352

276 Finally, the fourth circle of dialogue is carried out among the Catholic faithful, children of God’s house. This dialogue “does not mean that the virtue of obedience is no longer operative. The right to command and the duty to obey must be present.”353 Rather, it presumes obedience, because “the very exercise of authority becomes, in the context of this dialogue, an exercise of obedience, the obedient performance of a service, a ministry of truth and charity.”354

277 In order to be men of authentic dialogue, we must learn how to practice the following virtues: “Clarity before all else; the dialogue demands that what is said should be intelligible. We can think of it as a kind of thought transfusion… affability… It would indeed be a disgrace if our dialogue were marked by arrogance, the use of harsh words or offensive bitterness. What gives it authority is the fact that it affirms the truth, shares with others the gifts of charity, is itself an example of virtue, avoids peremptory language, makes no demands… Confidence is also necessary, confidence not only in the power of one’s own words, but also in the good will of both parties to dialogue. Hence dialogue promotes intimacy and friendship on both sides… Prudence of a teacher who is most careful to make allowances for the psychological and moral circumstances of his listener…355 The person who speaks always takes pains to learn the sensitivities of his audience, and if reason demands it, he adapts himself and the manner of his presentation to the susceptibilities and the degree of intelligence of his listeners.”356 “Moreover, the very fact that he engages in a dialogue of this sort is proof of his consideration and esteem for others, his understanding and his kindness. He detests bigotry and prejudice, malicious and indiscriminate hostility, and empty, boastful speech… True dialogue respects a man’s freedom and dignity… we nevertheless try to help him and to prepare him for a fuller sharing of ideas and convictions… Our dialogue, therefore, presupposes that we have a state of mind… that is characteristic of the man who realizes the seriousness of the apostolic mission…”357

278 We must also embrace the holy cause of ecumenism. There is a promise-prophecy of the Lord: There shall be one flock, one shepherd (Jn 10:16), and a prayer of the Lord, That they may all be one (Jn 17:21). By prayer, penance, study, dialogue, and collaboration, we must strive to reach full communion in the unity of the Church “which Christ bestowed on his Church from the beginning. We believe that this unity subsists in the Catholic Church as something she can never lose, and we hope that it will continue to increase until the end of time,”358 in order “that in a renewed conversion to the Lord, the following may become possible to all: to recognize the permanency of the Primacy of Peter in his successors, the Bishops of Rome, and that the Petrine ministry may be carried out just as it is understood by the Lord, as universal apostolic service, present in all the Churches from the inside, and that, preserving the substance of the Petrine ministry as a divine institution, it can be expressed in diverse ways...”359 The ecumenical commitment is to “pray and to work for reconciliation and for ecclesiastic unity according to the mind and heart of our Savior Jesus Christ.”360

g. The Apostolic Church

279 Another exciting reality of the immeasurable mystery of the Church of the Incarnate Word is its apostolicity: founded upon the Apostles and perpetuated by apostolic succession.

280 Besides being based on faith, baptism and Eucharist, the communion among the particular Churches in the universal Church is based on the Episcopacy. Church unity is also rooted in the unity of the Episcopacy: in order that the Church “might be one and undivided, Christ put Peter at the head of the other apostles, and in him He set up a lasting and visible source and foundation of the unity of both faith and communion.”361

281 “The individual bishops are the visible source and foundation of unity in their own particular Churches, which are established after the model of the universal Church.”362 For this to exist, the Church’s supreme authority, the College of Bishops “together with their head, the Supreme Pontiff, and never apart from him”363 must be present in the particular Church as a proper component. The Primacy of the Bishop of Rome and the College of Bishops are proper elements of the universal Church; they are not derived from the particular Churches, but are internal to each particular Church. “In the Pope we see Jesus Christ, we follow Jesus Christ, we love Jesus Christ. And in the Bishops? In the Bishops we see, we continue, we venerate and we love the successors of the Apostles.”364 Each one of the members of our Religious Family “wants to belong entirely to the Pope, the Bishops and the Church: worthless things, servants and obedient children of the Church, the Bishops and the Pope, in humility, with fidelity, with love without limits.”365

282 Therefore, we must have eyes of faith to always recognize those whom the Holy Spirit has made… overseers, to care for the church of the Lord (Acts 20:28). We must make the advice of Saint Ignatius of Antioch our own: “Neither do anything without the bishop and presbyters,”366 and even less so, something against them.

283 The Saint Louis Orione also advised: “The Bishop’s state is the most perfect of all, even more than the religious state; to him the fullness of the priesthood; to him more than to any other is given the spirit of Faith, Wisdom and Fortitude... The Bishop doesn’t have enemies; to him all are but children. The smallest ones, the most humble and the most disgraced ones are dearer to him. He prays for everyone. He has words of everlasting life for everyone. For everyone he goes to the altar and offers the blood of the Immaculate Lamb that takes away the sins of the world… The Bishop is the Good Shepherd who watches over, who tends the sheep, who evangelizes, who knows how to suffer in silence, who knows how to give his life up for his sheep.”367 Church history offers us numerous examples of glorious figures of the Episcopate: bishops who evangelized and founded nations, defended and organized peoples, keeping the deposit of faith entrusted to them368 amid the cruelest of persecutions, and who reinforced the Church’s sound doctrine in the face of a multitude of errors and confusions. For this reason, “Let us love the Bishops!”369

284 Not only is communion with the Bishop necessary, but we must also strive for communion with other priests “under the authority of the bishop,”370 who is God’s steward (Ti 1:7). This communion forms a single presbytery based on the common participation of Christ’s Priesthood: “In virtue of their sacred ordination and of their common mission, all priests are united together by bonds of intimate brotherhood, which manifests itself in a spontaneously and gladly-given mutual help, whether spiritual or temporal, whether pastoral or personal.”371

285 Unity with other priests, both diocesan and religious, is primarily obtained in the “intimate sacramental brotherhood”;372 and from this we wish to establish close collaboration in pastoral work, since “even though they have diverse occupations, they exercise a single priestly ministry in the service of men.”373 For this reason, “Between the secular clergy and the religious communities, a renewed brotherhood and a bond of cooperation must be encouraged; having in great esteem certain mutual help and certain contacts... that help mutual trust, apostolic unanimity and fraternal concord in such a great way…”374

286 This unity and cooperation which we want to establish with other members of the presbytery to whatever degree possible, leads us to preach Jesus Christ without any division,375 by word and example of life, and allows us to be aware that we are ministers of a new covenant, not in a written code but in the Spirit (2 Cor 3:6), and therefore it leads us to bear one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2) in this serious ministry.

287 Paraphrasing the Apostle,376 we want to do good always, to everyone, whenever possible, especially to our brothers in the priesthood bestowed by the laying on of hands.377

288 God’s marvelous gift of consecrated life – priests, deacons, religious, missionaries and consecrated lay people – “affects the whole Church in her fundamental mark of apostolicity.”378

289 The foundation of this essentially supernatural work resides in God’s very choice and call: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit (Jn 15:16); when choosing the Twelve, the Lord went up the mountain and summoned those whom he wanted, and they came to him (Mk 3:13). Vocations are God’s property: I pray for them. I do not pray for the world but for the ones you have given me, because they are yours, and everything of mine is yours and everything of yours is mine (Jn 17:9-10).

290 We would want God to give us the gift of being able to discover and to guide so many vocations that we would fill all the good seminaries and novitiates in the entire world, according to the Pope’s recommendation: “God calls who he wants, by his free initiative of love. But he wants to call through us... There shouldn’t be any fear in directly proposing the Lord’s call to a young person.”379 Therefore, vocational ministry should be active, constant, full of energy and vitality, undertaken and spurred forward by the charity of Christ,380 and definitely opposed to a mentality of “ordinary administration or bureaucratic slowness,”381 which carelessly hopes that vocations knock upon its door. God “sows seeds of vocation to full hands by grace.”382

291 The vitality of a community, and of the Church herself, can be measured by the vocations that God raises in it. Inseparably united with promoting vocations is the proper formation of those chosen; hence, we must recognize the importance “of making intense efforts to encourage vocations and to offer the best possible priestly formation in seminaries. An abundance of vocations and an effective formation of seminarians are two tests of the Church’s vitality.”383

292 The task of discovering and guiding vocations is achieved not only through an enthusiastic pastoral action, but essentially through prayer: Pray, therefore, the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Mt 9:38); I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Cor 3:6). One’s example and life testimony go together with prayer: “Where there is faith, prayer, charity, apostolate, Christian life, there the gifts of God multiply,”384 because “the religious and priests who live their vocation calmly day by day, faithful to their commitments, humble and hidden builders of the Kingdom of God from whose words, behavior, and life irradiates the luminous joy of the choice that they made... are in fact... those that by their example will stimulate many to welcome in their hearts the charism of vocation.”385

293 Hence all anti-testimony, all incoherence between expressing values or ideals and living them, all looking out for oneself and not for the Kingdom of God and its justice,386 all falsification of the word of God,387 “are often strong obstacles for those who feel the call of Christ: Come and follow me.”388

h. In the “Three White Things”389 The Eucharist

294 Ecclesial communion has its root and its center in the Holy Eucharist. The Eucharist is the source and creative force of communion among the Church’s members because it unites each one with the same Christ: “Really sharing in the body of the Lord in the breaking of the Eucharistic bread, we are taken up into communion with Him and with one another. Because the bread is one, we, though many, are one body, all of us who partake of the one bread (1 Cor 10:17).”390 “The common spiritual good of the whole Church is contained substantially391 in the sacrament of the Eucharist itself,” “which is Christ.”392

295 The Church is the Body of Christ. This means that in the Eucharist, in which the Lord gives His Body and transforms us into one Body393, the Church permanently expresses herself in her most essential form: present everywhere at the same time, one like Christ.

296 In the Eucharist all the faithful find themselves “in their own Church”, since in all valid Eucharistic celebrations, the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church becomes present. The faithful are indeed “in their own Church” even though, from a canonical point of view, they may or may not belong to the particular diocese, parish or community where the celebration is being carried out.

297 Besides being based on faith, Baptism and Episcopacy, – the communion of specific Churches in the universal Church is fundamentally based upon the Eucharist. Since in the Eucharist we receive the Lord and His gift of salvation, the Eucharistic Sacrifice never belongs to a particular community. Each community is thereby manifested – beyond its visible particularity – as an image and true presence of the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church.394

298 The unity and indivisibility of the Eucharistic Body of the Lord implies the unity and indivisibility of the mystical Body of the Lord. Each Eucharist makes us surrender to the Lord, and integrates us into His one and undivided Body. That is why the Petrine ministry – the foundation of unity between the Episcopate and the universal Church – corresponds deeply with the Church’s Eucharistic dimension.

299 Since Eucharist and Episcopate are realities essentially linked395 by the institution of Christ, the unity of the Eucharist and the unity of the Episcopacy “with Peter and under Peter”396 are not independent roots of the Church’s unity. The liturgy manifests this reality, since all Eucharistic celebrations are carried out in union with one’s own Bishop, the Pope, the universal Episcopate, the clergy and all the members of the People of God.397 All valid celebrations of the Eucharist either express this universal communion with Peter and with the whole Church, or at least claim it objectively, as in the case of the Churches separated from Rome.

300 Therefore, in the Eucharist, the perpetuation of the sacrifice of the Cross, we will always find the deepest foundation of our unity as a Religious Family. The Eucharist must be one of our great loves, since it is the undeniable sign of God’s immeasurable love for men, it is the sign of a God who wants to remain among men and who gives Himself up to man totally: “In the Sacrament, the logic of the Incarnation reaches its extreme consequences.”398

301 The primary role of a priest is sacrifice: “A holy and unblemished sacrifice,”399 “acceptable... which brings salvation to the whole world”400 that “opens a way” toward the Father for us,401 “unique,”402 “of perfect reconciliation,”403 “ours,”404 “living.”405 Therefore, in the Eucharistic Liturgy Christ speaks, above all, with the strength of His Sacrifice. His speech is very concise but ardent. We must know how to listen to it attentively.

302 Every month a Holy Mass must be offered for the deceased members of the Institute, another one for the intentions of the General Superior, and a third one requesting the grace of final perseverance for all the members of our Institutes.

The Virgin Mary

303 The Virgin Mary should be another one of our great loves because of her union with Christ and with the Church. Since She gave birth to the Head, She gave birth to us members as well. She was given to us as Mother when She was standing at the foot of the Cross: Behold, your son (Jn 19:26).

304 The Holy Virgin Mary is model of ecclesial communion “in the order of faith, charity, and perfect union with Christ”;406 She “is the image and beginning of the Church… She shines forth on earth, as a sign of sure hope and solace to the people of God during its sojourn on earth.”407

305 She is in the midst of the Apostles, at the very heart of the newborn Church: All these with one accord devoted themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers (Acts 1:14), and She is in the heart of the Church for all ages.

306 Indeed, “The Church was congregated in the upper part (of the cenacle) with Mary, who was the Mother of Jesus, and with his brethren. We cannot therefore speak of the Church unless Mary, the Mother of the Lord, is present there, with the Lord’s brethren.”408 The Marian dimension is as essential to the one Church of Christ as are the Eucharistic and Petrine dimensions.

307 We must be apostles of Mary giving ourselves up to Her in a filial slavery of love, and doing everything “through Mary, with Mary, in Mary and for Mary.”409

308 Always keep a memory of the Blessed Virgin in mind during eutrapelia and during cultural activities, because, after Jesus Christ, no one has done as much for the evangelization of culture as She did.

The Pope

309 Our third great love must always be the “white figure” of the Pope. “Wherever Peter is, the Church is there,”410 and “Peter has spoken thus through Leo”411 (at the moment of the writing of this Directory, through Blessed John Paul II). After Simon gives testimony of Christ, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Mt 16:16), Christ gives testimony of Simon: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church (Mt 16:18).

310 The idea of a Body of Churches demands the existence of a Head of these Churches. It is the Church of Rome, which “presides over the universal communion of love.”412 Peter’s Successor “is the perpetual and visible source and foundation”413 of the unity of the universal Church and of the unity of the Episcopate. Hence the Petrine ministry is not a service that reaches to the particular Churches “from outside,” but one “already belonging to the essence of each particular Church from inside.”414 The ministry of Primacy implies an Episcopal power – both as universal Bishop and as Bishop of the Diocese of Rome – and not merely an episcopal dignity, so that everything a Bishop can do in his parishes, the Pope can do in all of the local Churches. This ministry is a supreme power: no one possesses equal or greater power; it is a full power, not merely a principal part; it is immediate – the Pope can exercise this power over the Bishops and the faithful; it is universal, over all without excluding anyone; it is ordinary, derived directly from Jesus Christ; and “he can always exercise it unhindered.”415

311 The primordial task of the Roman Pontiff for the whole Church is to promote unity that is not contrary to promoting the diversification needed for proper communion.

312 We make the teaching of Saint Ignatius of Loyola our own: “If we wish to proceed securely in all things, we must hold fast to the following principle: What seems to me white, I will believe black if the hierarchical Church so defines.”416 Therefore, being certain that this is the will of Jesus Christ, “Let us remain deaf when someone speaks to us disregarding the Pope, or not explicitly in favor of the Pope, and when one is not in favor of the Church’s wholesome and precise doctrine; these are not fruits of the Heavenly Father, but wicked sprouts of heresies that produce murderous fruit.”417 Let us always remember “that the Pope should be loved in the cross; and whoever does not love him in the cross, does not seriously love him. To be in everything with the Pope means to be in everything with God; to love Jesus Christ and to love the Pope is the same love,”418 since “to love the Pope, to love the Church, is to love Jesus Christ.”419

Article 6: His Second Coming a. Antecedent Signs

313 Jesus Christ came for the first time in humility and poverty. However, He will come a second time in power, greatness, dignity and majesty to demand an account and to judge.

314 The major signs of His second coming are three:

1. the Gospel will be preached to the whole world;420

2. there will be a universal apostasy;421

3. the Antichrist will make His appearance.422

315 There will come a time when men will go astray from the truth and will delight in iniquity,423 a time in which the majority will not have true faith in Jesus Christ. The certainty that this universal apostasy will happen one day must prevent us from joining the triumphant march of any movement or ideology that is set apart from Christ, although it may seem that the whole world is following it. We must always follow Christ, and even though the enemies seem to be in the majority, we must say: “We are surrounded everywhere, don’t let them escape.” “All creatures appear small to the soul that contemplates God.”424

b. The Final and Universal Resurrection

316 At the end of time the resurrection of the body will take place. All men and women will resurrect by the power of God. We believe in the resurrection, and we are not afraid of persecutors who stalk the Church: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Mt 10:28).

317 The time of this resurrection is hidden and “all those who had been misled to calculate the aforesaid time have so far proved to be untruthful.”425

318 The soul will take up its own entire body, and will enjoy the gifts of impassibility, subtlety, agility and clarity – or beauty.

319 Our trust and happiness from knowing that death has already been conquered should be so great! It has been conquered by the Incarnation of the Word and His redeeming Sacrifice. The Incarnation of the Word is the condition and guarantee for the whole universe: “The lack of life and salvation from despair for all men, the condition sine qua non and the guarantee for the whole universe are locked in the words, The Word was made flesh and the faith in these words.”426 “The Incarnation of the Son of God is the foundation, the source and the pattern of a new supernatural order of existence for all men; in fact, from this mystery they obtain the grace that sanctifies and saves them, and it is a foundation of Christian anthropology that is also projected in the natural sphere of thought and life, with its exaltation of man as person, placed in the center of society and, you can say, of the whole world.”427

c. The Parousia and the Final Judgment

320 Then, the Parousia of the Lord will happen: For the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (Jn 5:28). And then they will see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory (Lk 21:27); the sign of the Son of man [the sign of the Cross] in heaven will appear (Mt 24:30). At that moment the universal judgment will take place. Christ, together with His chosen ones – you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Mt 19:28) – will separate the sheep from the goats; some will be put to His right, and others to His left; and He will say, Come, O blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom… (Mt 25:34), and depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire (Mt 25:41). And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Mt 25:46).

321 We must increasingly convince ourselves that we do not work for ephemeral or fleeting things, but “for the most divine work among the divine ones,”428 which is the eternal salvation of souls and the glorious resurrection of bodies. Aware that we are working for eternal life, we must say with Blessed Louis Orione, “Place me, Lord, on the mouth of hell, so that I, by your mercy, may close it.”429

d. The Innovation

322 Then, the renewal of the entire material universe will take place. There will be a new heaven and a new earth (Is 65:17; Rev 21:1), so that the man resurrected in glory will be able to clearly see divinity with His senses, and somehow, he will see it in the corporeal world. The following words will be entirely true: “The heaven, and earth, and all that is therein, behold, on every side; they say that I should love You.”430

323 The quantity and mode of this renewal “is known to Him alone Who will bring it about.”431 There God…[will] be everything to everyone (1 Cor 15:28); matter will reach maximum dignity, manifesting the Divine Spirit, because it will be a perfect mirror of God.

324 We only need to pray, work and wait, knowing that this world is passing away (1 Cor 7:31).

CHAPTER 3 EPILOGUE

325 We finish this part of our fundamental code by summarizing what we want to be our spirituality:

Not Jesus or Mary; not Mary or Jesus. Neither Jesus without Mary; nor Mary without Jesus. Neither only Jesus, but also Mary; not only Mary, but also Jesus. Always Jesus and Mary; always Mary and Jesus.

To Mary through Jesus: Behold, your mother! (Jn 19:27).

To Jesus through Mary: Do whatever he tells you (Jn 2:5). First Jesus, the God man; then Mary, the Mother of God. He, the Head; She, the Neck; we, the Body.

Everything through Jesus and through Mary; with Jesus and with Mary; in Jesus and in Mary; for Jesus and for Mary.

In short, simply: Jesus and Mary; Mary and Jesus.

And through Christ, to the Father, in the Holy Spirit.
